text:
About Lyme Disease — What Is Lyme Disease

Lyme disease is a bacterial infection spread to people through the bite of infected blacklegged ticks. In the United States, it is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi and, rarely, Borrelia mayonii.

metadata.source_name: About Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: About Lyme Disease > What Is Lyme Disease

text:
About Lyme Disease — How Common It Is

It is the most common vector-borne illness reported in the United States and is most frequently reported in the Northeast, mid-Atlantic, and upper-Midwest regions, where infected ticks are most common in forested and grassy areas.

metadata.source_name: About Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: About Lyme Disease > How Common It Is

text:
Clinical Care of Lyme Disease — Standard Treatment

Lyme disease is generally treated with a course of oral antibiotics. Early diagnosis and proper antibiotic treatment are important and can help prevent more serious symptoms from developing.

metadata.source_name: Clinical Care of Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: Clinical Care of Lyme Disease > Standard Treatment

text:
Clinical Care of Lyme Disease — Commonly Used Antibiotics

Commonly used antibiotics include doxycycline, amoxicillin, and cefuroxime; the specific choice and duration depend on the patient's age, symptoms, and stage of disease. Most people treated in the early stages recover quickly and completely.

metadata.source_name: Clinical Care of Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: Clinical Care of Lyme Disease > Commonly Used Antibiotics

text:
How Lyme Disease Spreads — Tick Transmission

Lyme disease is spread to people through the bite of an infected blacklegged tick (also called a deer tick).

metadata.source_name: How Lyme Disease Spreads
metadata.section_path: How Lyme Disease Spreads > Tick Transmission

text:
How Lyme Disease Spreads — Attachment Time and Risk

In most cases, a tick needs to be attached for more than 24 hours before it can transmit the Lyme disease bacteria, so finding and removing an attached tick promptly can reduce the risk of infection.

metadata.source_name: How Lyme Disease Spreads
metadata.section_path: How Lyme Disease Spreads > Attachment Time and Risk

text:
Preventing Lyme Disease — Avoiding Tick Bites

The best way to prevent Lyme disease is to avoid tick bites. 5% permethrin, and checking your body for ticks after spending time outdoors.

metadata.source_name: Preventing Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: Preventing Lyme Disease > Avoiding Tick Bites

text:
Preventing Lyme Disease — Removing Ticks Promptly

Ticks should be removed as soon as possible, since delaying removal increases the risk of infection.

metadata.source_name: Preventing Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: Preventing Lyme Disease > Removing Ticks Promptly

metadata.source_name: Signs and Symptoms of Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: Signs and Symptoms of Lyme Disease > Early Symptoms

text:
Signs and Symptoms of Lyme Disease — Symptoms If Left Untreated

If left untreated, the infection can spread from the site of the bite to other parts of the body, producing a wider range of symptoms including facial palsy, arthritis (especially in the knees), heart rhythm irregularities, and nervous system problems.

metadata.source_name: Signs and Symptoms of Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: Signs and Symptoms of Lyme Disease > Symptoms If Left Untreated

text:
Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease — Two-Tiered Blood Testing

CDC recommends a standard two-step (two-tiered) blood testing process to help diagnose Lyme disease: a first-tier enzyme-linked immunoassay (ELISA) test, followed by a second, more specific Western blot test only if the first result is positive or equivocal. If the first test is negative, no further testing is recommended.

metadata.source_name: Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease > Two-Tiered Blood Testing

text:
Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease — Limitations of Testing

These tests detect antibodies to the Lyme disease bacteria, so results can be falsely negative in the first few weeks after infection, before the body has produced enough antibodies.

metadata.source_name: Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease > Limitations of Testing

text:
Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease — Antibody Response Timing

Standard two-tier Lyme disease testing detects the body's antibody response to the infection, not the bacterium itself. The IgM antibody response typically peaks 3 to 6 weeks after infection and may not be detectable in the first two weeks. As a result, the sensitivity of testing at first presentation (early illness) is estimated at roughly 22-36%, meaning a real, active infection can still produce a negative test result if the test is drawn too early in the course of illness.

metadata.source_name: Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease > Antibody Response Timing

text:
Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease — Retesting Guidance

CDC recommends repeat testing 2 to 4 weeks later when the first test was taken before the body has had time to develop an adequate antibody response, so an early negative result is not the end of the process for someone with a compatible exposure and symptom history.

metadata.source_name: Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease
metadata.section_path: Testing and Diagnosis for Lyme Disease > Retesting Guidance

text:
Tick-Borne Co-Infections — Why Co-Infection Matters

The same blacklegged tick that spreads Lyme disease can also carry other pathogens, including Babesia (which causes babesiosis) and Anaplasma (which causes anaplasmosis), as well as Borrelia miyamotoi. A person can be infected with more than one of these at the same time from a single tick bite. Untreated co-infection is a documented reason some patients do not fully improve after standard Lyme disease treatment, since Lyme antibiotics do not necessarily treat these other infections.

metadata.source_name: Tick-Borne Co-Infections
metadata.section_path: Tick-Borne Co-Infections > Why Co-Infection Matters

text:
Tick-Borne Co-Infections — Babesiosis Signals

Babesiosis symptoms can overlap with Lyme disease but also include some distinct signals: drenching night sweats (soaking through clothing or bedding) and air hunger (a sensation of not being able to get a full breath, distinct from ordinary shortness of breath). These are not symptoms typically emphasized in Lyme disease alone, and their presence is a reasonable question to raise with a clinician about testing for babesiosis.

metadata.source_name: Tick-Borne Co-Infections
metadata.section_path: Tick-Borne Co-Infections > Babesiosis Signals

text:
Tick-Borne Co-Infections — Anaplasmosis Signals

Anaplasmosis often presents with a high fever together with low blood cell counts (cytopenias, such as low white blood cells or platelets) found on routine bloodwork. A high fever combined with abnormal blood counts, especially following a known or possible tick exposure, is a reasonable question to raise with a clinician about testing for anaplasmosis.

metadata.source_name: Tick-Borne Co-Infections
metadata.section_path: Tick-Borne Co-Infections > Anaplasmosis Signals
